negative: It takes 1 hour to get there, or 1.5 hours, or 10 hours.

reason: After a number above one the unit is plural: “5 tonnes”.
positive: The truck carries 5 tonne of sand.
negative: The truck carries 5 tonnes of sand. A 5 tonne walk and a 1 tonne wait are fine.

reason: After a number above one the unit is plural: “12 volts”.
positive: The battery gives 12 volt of power.
negative: The battery gives 12 volts of power. A 12 volt gap is fine.

reason: After a number above one the unit is plural: “60 watts”.
positive: The lamp uses 60 watt of power.
negative: The lamp uses 60 watts of power. A 60 watt gap is fine.

reason: After a number above one the unit is plural: “4 weeks”.
positive: The course runs 4 week in total.
negative: The course runs 4 weeks in total. A 4 week walk and a 1 week wait are fine.

reason: Use the adjective “wide” after a measurement: “10 meters wide”.
positive: The pool is 25 meters width.
negative: The pool is 25 meters wide, and the rope is 25 meters in width.

reason: After a number above one the unit is plural: “5 yards”.
positive: The goal is 5 yard away.
negative: The goal is 5 yards away. A 5 yard walk and a 1 yard wait are fine.

reason: After a number above one the unit is plural: “10 years”.
positive: The lease runs 10 year in total.
negative: The lease runs 10 years in total. A 10 year walk and a 1 year wait are fine.

reason: After “a couple of” the noun is plural: “a couple of days”.
positive: He left a couple of day ago.
negative: He left a couple of days ago, and a couple of day-trips went well.

reason: The number is spelt “fourteen”.
positive: He turned forteen last week.
negative: He turned fourteen last week, and she turned forty.

reason: The ordinal for 4 is “fourth”; “forth” means “forward”.
positive: This is the forth time I asked.
negative: This is the fourth time I asked, and he walked back and forth.

reason: “o’clock” is only used for a full hour: “half past five”, not “half past five o’clock”.
positive: We left at half past five o'clock sharp.
negative: We left at half past five sharp, or at five o'clock sharp.

reason: Compound numbers from 21 to 99 are written with a hyphen: “twenty-one”.
positive: She ate twentyone grapes.
negative: She ate twenty-one grapes, and twenty grapes more.

reason: After an exact number no “of” is needed: “a thousand people”.
positive: A thousand of people signed it.
negative: A thousand people signed it, and a thousand of the people signed it.

reason: The number is spelt “seventeen”.
positive: She turned sevnteen last week.
negative: She turned seventeen last week, and he turned seventy.

reason: After “several”, “many” or “a few” the unit is plural: “a few miles”.
positive: It is a few mile from here.
negative: It is a few miles from here, and a mile-long queue formed.

reason: After “tens of” or “hundreds of” the big number is plural: “tens of thousands”.
positive: Tens of thousand of people came.
negative: Tens of thousands of people came, and hundreds of thousands watched.
